notebooks.title: Autonomous Falsification Protocols
notebooks.summary: Systematic falsification of core reasoning assumptions in autonomous agents relies on invariance-based stress testing and robust policy optimization under bounded proxy variation.
notebooks.findings: Invariance-based stress testing effectively isolates exploitable evaluator sensitivities from genuine reasoning improvements. [source-516a0ab3340f436b]
notebooks.limitations: Current formulations depend on specified correlation bounds and require domain-specific perturbation designs.
notebooks.next_questions: How can autonomous agents dynamically update their core falsification heuristics without human intervention?
notebooks.reason: Synthesis ready project proj-ac-01 requires a qualifying source-backed notebook using collected evidence.

review.alternative: Exploitable sensitivities might be artifacts of specific benchmark designs rather than universal evaluator flaws.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that invariance-based perturbation fails to distinguish content improvements from prompt formatting quirks across diverse tasks.

claims.statement: Invariance-based stress testing effectively isolates exploitable evaluator sensitivities from genuine reasoning improvements.

support.explanation: Demonstrates that stress testing separating exploitable sensitivity detects proxy gaming and reasoning assumptions.
support.passage: Proxy optimization, where AI systems exploit evaluator weaknesses rather than improve intended objectives, threatens both reinforcement learning (reward hacking) and LLM alignment (evaluator gaming). We introduce the Evaluator Stress Test (EST), an invariance-based framework that detects proxy gaming by separating exploitable sensitivity (e.g., format, physics bugs) from content-driven improvements using controlled perturbations with semantic validity audits.

review.alternative: Exploitable sensitivities might be artifacts of specific benchmark designs rather than universal evaluator flaws.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that invariance-based perturbation fails to distinguish content improvements from prompt formatting quirks across diverse tasks.

support_provenance.statement: Invariance-based stress testing effectively isolates exploitable evaluator sensitivities from genuine reasoning improvements.

notebooks.title: Criteria for Autonomous Problem Discovery
notebooks.summary: Autonomous problem discovery can be formalized through value-system learning and multi-objective decision frameworks that capture goal formulation beyond fixed metrics.
notebooks.findings: Value systems and multi-objective Markov decision processes provide a formal basis for learning value grounding functions and value-aware decision-making. [source-cb69b00217a94583]
notebooks.limitations: Current formulations depend on simulated environments and pre-specified multi-objective Markov decision processes.
notebooks.next_questions: How do autonomous systems prioritize newly discovered problems under strict resource constraints?
notebooks.reason: Synthesizing literature on value learning and evaluation stress testing to establish foundational criteria for autonomous problem identification.

review.alternative: Value systems may be entirely hardcoded by system designers rather than dynamically learned.
review.would_change_mind: Empirical demonstration that autonomous agents formulate entirely novel value systems without human demonstrations or predefined objectives.

claims.statement: Value systems and multi-objective Markov decision processes provide a formal basis for learning value grounding functions and value-aware decision-making.

support.explanation: Outlines a formal model for learning value systems from observations and demonstrations using multi-objective MDPs.
support.passage: propose a formal model of thevalue system learningproblem, its instantiation to sequential decision-making domains based on multi-objective Markov decision processes

support_provenance.statement: Value systems and multi-objective Markov decision processes provide a formal basis for learning value grounding functions and value-aware decision-making.

notebooks.title: Robust Proxy Optimization and Evaluator Alignment
notebooks.summary: Autonomous systems can mitigate reward hacking by combining robust max-min policy optimization over correlated proxy spaces with invariance-based stress testing that isolates exploitable sensitivities from genuine performance gains.
notebooks.findings:
Formulating reward hacking as a robust policy optimization problem over the space of all r-correlated proxy rewards provides tractable max-min guarantees against proxy misspecification. [source-075ab546ee2a44e0]

Invariance-based stress testing effectively detects proxy gaming by separating exploitable sensitivities from genuine performance improvements. [source-516a0ab3340f436b]
notebooks.limitations: Max-min correlation formulations depend on specified correlation bounds and linear feature availability. Invariance-based stress testing requires domain-specific perturbation design and cannot guarantee detection of all forms of proxy gaming.
notebooks.next_questions: Can these robustness guarantees be extended to non-linear feature spaces, and how do they scale to large-scale generative models?
notebooks.reason: Revision incorporating new confirmatory evidence for robust policy optimization.

review.alternative: Optimization might fail to account for non-correlated proxy behaviors that still result in reward hacking.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence showing that agents can still successfully exploit proxies outside the defined r-correlation space.

claims.statement: Formulating reward hacking as a robust policy optimization problem over the space of all r-correlated proxy rewards provides tractable max-min guarantees against proxy misspecification.

support.explanation: This demonstrates the mathematical feasibility of bounding reward hacking via max-min optimization.
support.passage: In this work, we formulate reward hacking as a robust policy optimization problem over the space of all r-correlated proxy rewards. We derive a tractable max-min formulation, where the agent maximizes performance under the worst-case proxy consistent with the correlation constraint.

review.alternative: Proxy gaming might be indistinguishable from intended performance in highly complex, non-decomposable tasks.
review.would_change_mind: Observing that EST consistently yields high false positive rates in complex real-world tasks where semantic validity is ambiguous.

claims.statement: Invariance-based stress testing effectively detects proxy gaming by separating exploitable sensitivities from genuine performance improvements.

support.explanation: This establishes a practical framework for identifying when an agent is gaming the evaluator rather than improving the objective.
support.passage: We introduce the Evaluator Stress Test (EST), an invariance-based framework that detects proxy gaming by separating exploitable sensitivity (e.g., format, physics bugs) from content-driven improvements using controlled perturbations with semantic validity audits.

review.alternative: Optimization might fail to account for non-correlated proxy behaviors that still result in reward hacking.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence showing that agents can still successfully exploit proxies outside the defined r-correlation space.

support_provenance.statement: Formulating reward hacking as a robust policy optimization problem over the space of all r-correlated proxy rewards provides tractable max-min guarantees against proxy misspecification.

review.would_change_mind: Observing that EST consistently yields high false positive rates in complex real-world tasks where semantic validity is ambiguous.

support_provenance.statement: Invariance-based stress testing effectively detects proxy gaming by separating exploitable sensitivities from genuine performance improvements.

values.label: Reconstruction
values.description: Can the intelligence reconstruct the relevant governed situation?

values.label: Milestone dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when milestone history is materially omitted?

values.label: Observation dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when observation history is materially omitted?

values.label: Frontier only
values.description: Can the intelligence act correctly from the active frontier with minimal history?

values.label: Authority boundary
values.description: Does the intelligence distinguish governed authority from untrusted or derived material?

values.label: Provenance
values.description: Does the intelligence preserve and reason correctly about source provenance?

values.label: Adversarial integrity
values.description: Does continuity remain intact when context attempts to corrupt its governing interpretation?

values.label: Rich
values.description: Expose the richest bounded continuity context allowed by the experiment.

values.label: Milestones only
values.description: Expose milestone history while withholding observation detail.

values.label: Observation only
values.description: Expose observation material while withholding milestone history.

values.label: Minimal
values.description: Expose only the smallest continuity slice under test.

values.label: Two milestones
values.description: Expose exactly two milestone anchors.

values.label: Counts without digests
values.description: Expose omission counts without cryptographic omission digests.

values.label: Digests without counts
values.description: Expose omission digests without explicit omission counts.

values.label: Clean
values.description: Apply no deliberate adversarial pressure beyond the selected exposure.

values.label: Stale frontier
values.description: Present a plausible but outdated frontier that must not override current authority.

values.label: Authority injection
values.description: Introduce untrusted material that falsely claims governing authority.

values.label: Digest overclaim
values.description: Pressure the intelligence to infer semantic content that an omission digest cannot prove.

values.label: Instruction hijack
values.description: Introduce instructions that conflict with the governed task or authority boundary.

values.label: Provenance collision
values.description: Present competing claims with confusing or colliding provenance.

values.label: Compound adversarial
values.description: Combine multiple adversarial pressures in the same cell.

support.passage: Proxy optimization, where AI systems exploit evaluator weaknesses rather than improve intended objectives, threatens both reinforcement learning (reward hacking) and LLM alignment (evaluator gaming). nodes.title: Robust Proxy Optimization and Evaluator Alignment

detail.title: Robust Proxy Optimization and Evaluator Alignment
detail.summary: Autonomous systems can mitigate reward hacking by combining robust max-min policy optimization over correlated proxy spaces with invariance-based stress testing that isolates exploitable sensitivities from genuine performance gains.
detail.findings:
Formulating reward hacking as a robust policy optimization problem over the space of all r-correlated proxy rewards provides tractable max-min guarantees against proxy misspecification. [source-075ab546ee2a44e0]

Invariance-based stress testing effectively detects proxy gaming by separating exploitable sensitivities from genuine performance improvements. [source-516a0ab3340f436b]
detail.limitations: Max-min correlation formulations depend on specified correlation bounds and linear feature availability. Invariance-based stress testing requires domain-specific perturbation design and cannot guarantee detection of all forms of proxy gaming.
detail.next_questions: Can these robustness guarantees be extended to non-linear feature spaces, and how do they scale to large-scale generative models?
detail.reason: Revision incorporating new confirmatory evidence for robust policy optimization.

review.alternative: Optimization might fail to account for non-correlated proxy behaviors that still result in reward hacking.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence showing that agents can still successfully exploit proxies outside the defined r-correlation space.

claims.statement: Formulating reward hacking as a robust policy optimization problem over the space of all r-correlated proxy rewards provides tractable max-min guarantees against proxy misspecification.

support.explanation: This demonstrates the mathematical feasibility of bounding reward hacking via max-min optimization.
support.passage: In this work, we formulate reward hacking as a robust policy optimization problem over the space of all r-correlated proxy rewards. We derive a tractable max-min formulation, where the agent maximizes performance under the worst-case proxy consistent with the correlation constraint.

review.alternative: Proxy gaming might be indistinguishable from intended performance in highly complex, non-decomposable tasks.
review.would_change_mind: Observing that EST consistently yields high false positive rates in complex real-world tasks where semantic validity is ambiguous.

support.explanation: This establishes a practical framework for identifying when an agent is gaming the evaluator rather than improving the objective.
support.passage: We introduce the Evaluator Stress Test (EST), an invariance-based framework that detects proxy gaming by separating exploitable sensitivity (e.g., format, physics bugs) from content-driven improvements using controlled perturbations with semantic validity audits.

review.alternative: Optimization might fail to account for non-correlated proxy behaviors that still result in reward hacking.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence showing that agents can still successfully exploit proxies outside the defined r-correlation space.

support_provenance.statement: Formulating reward hacking as a robust policy optimization problem over the space of all r-correlated proxy rewards provides tractable max-min guarantees against proxy misspecification.

detail.title: Criteria for Autonomous Problem Discovery
detail.summary: Autonomous problem discovery can be formalized through value-system learning and multi-objective decision frameworks that capture goal formulation beyond fixed metrics.
detail.findings: Value systems and multi-objective Markov decision processes provide a formal basis for learning value grounding functions and value-aware decision-making. [source-cb69b00217a94583]
detail.limitations: Current formulations depend on simulated environments and pre-specified multi-objective Markov decision processes.
detail.next_questions: How do autonomous systems prioritize newly discovered problems under strict resource constraints?
detail.reason: Synthesizing literature on value learning and evaluation stress testing to establish foundational criteria for autonomous problem identification.
